summary: RELOAD is a peer-to-peer signaling protocol that builds an overlay to store and retrieve data. This document describes how its default topology plugin can be extended to self-tune, adapting to changing conditions such as churn and network size.

eli5.summary: In a group of friends passing messages, people leave and join all the time. This RFC lets the group adjust itself automatically so messages still reach the right person quickly.

questions: what is self-tuning dht in reload
how does reload estimate overlay size
subtitle: How a RELOAD peer-to-peer overlay can measure its own size and churn and tune its maintenance traffic to match.

tldr.problem: A distributed hash table needs regular maintenance to keep routing state correct while peers come and go. Fixed settings cannot give both a low failure rate and low overhead when network size and churn change.
tldr.mechanism: Each peer estimates overlay size, failure rate and join rate, shares those estimates with a few other peers, and uses them to set its stabilization interval and the sizes of its routing structures.
tldr.outcome: Operators no longer have to guess every DHT parameter in advance. The feature is optional, but when an overlay uses it, all peers must support it.

today: RFC 7363 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and it builds on RFC 6940, the RELOAD base protocol.

sections.title: Adding Self-Tuning to RELOAD
sections.content:
RELOAD (RFC 6940) is a peer-to-peer signaling protocol. Peers form an overlay network, store data in it and retrieve data from it. For interoperability, RELOAD makes one overlay algorithm mandatory to implement, called chord-reload.

RFC 7363 extends chord-reload with self-tuning behavior. Using it is optional, but when an overlay uses it, every peer in the overlay needs to support it. The overlay announces this in its configuration document by naming the algorithm CHORD-SELF-TUNING in the topology-plugin element.

The RFC names two benefits: users no longer have to tune every DHT parameter correctly for a given environment, and the system adapts when conditions change.
sections.eli5: RELOAD is a way for lots of computers to share a big phone book without a boss. This RFC teaches them to adjust how often they check on each other, so nobody has to set it by hand.

sections.title: Why Stabilization Needs Tuning
sections.content:
DHTs use stabilization routines to keep each peer's routing information consistent with a topology that keeps changing because of churn (peers joining and leaving). There are two approaches. In reactive stabilization a peer reacts to the loss or arrival of a neighbor by sending its neighbor table around. In periodic stabilization a peer shares its neighborhood set on a timer, whatever has changed.

The RFC cites work showing that reactive stabilization works for small overlays with moderate churn, but in large overlays (the example given is 1000 peers or more) or under high churn it risks a positive feedback cycle that can end in congestion collapse. That is why most DHTs use periodic stabilization.

Periodic stabilization has its own problem: choosing the rate. A high rate detects changes quickly but costs traffic. A low rate with high churn leaves routing tables inaccurate and can even partition the network. Static configuration only works when conditions are known in advance and never change. A self-tuning DHT instead has each peer collect statistics and adjust its stabilization rate, neighborhood set size and finger table size.

The RFC gives a worked example: for a 500-peer overlay where one peer joins and one leaves every 30 seconds, an appropriate interval is on the order of 93 s. If churn doubles, it drops to about 46 s.
sections.eli5: If you check on your friends too often you waste time, and if you check too rarely you miss that someone left. The best rate depends on how fast the group is changing, so the group should work it out as it goes.

sections.title: Chord Basics
sections.content:
Chord uses consistent hashing to build a DHT from independent peers. Peers and resources get fixed-length identifiers, generated with SHA-1 as the base hash function. In RELOAD the identifier length is numBitsInNodeId = 128 bits. Identifiers are ordered on a circle called the Chord ring, and a key is assigned to the first peer whose identifier equals or follows the key.

To avoid passing a query around the ring one successor at a time, each peer keeps a finger table with up to numBitsInNodeId entries. The first entry points to a peer halfway around the ring, the second a quarter of the way, and so on. A peer keeps information about O(log(N)) other peers; for N=100000 the RFC says 17 fingers are sufficient.

For robustness each peer also keeps a successor list of its first r successors, and a predecessor list. If peers fail independently with probability p, all r successors fail together with probability only p^r. The routing table is the finger table plus the successor and predecessor lists.
sections.eli5: Picture everyone standing in a big circle. Each person knows their close neighbors and a few people far across the circle, so a message can jump across quickly instead of being passed hand to hand.

sections.title: Changes to chord-reload Stabilization
sections.content:
Self-tuning uses the periodic recovery strategy. Stabilization in chord-reload has four components: neighbor stabilization, finger stabilization, adjusting the finger table size, and detecting partitioning. The defaults in RELOAD base are an Update to every connected peer every ten minutes for neighbors, and one hour for fingers. This document makes those intervals adaptive.

  • Update requests: every Update request MUST carry an uptime field in seconds. Because each peer sizes its own lists, the predecessors, successors and fingers fields are variable length, with two length bytes and 16-byte NodeId entries. A peer MUST ignore extra entries it cannot fit.
  • Neighbor stabilization: a peer sends periodic Update requests of type neighbors only to its first predecessor and first successor, and MUST NOT send them to others. A new neighbor gets a peer_ready Update.
  • Finger stabilization: either of the two chord-reload search methods still works. After adding a new finger, the peer sends a Probe asking for uptime.
  • Finger table size: the network size estimate replaces the chord-reload mechanism.
  • Partition detection: unchanged.
  • Leaving: a leaving peer SHOULD send Leave requests carrying a ChordLeaveData structure. Successors receive its predecessor list and predecessors receive its successor list.
sections.eli5: Instead of calling everyone you know, you now only call the person just before you and just after you in the circle, and they pass news along. Newcomers also tell you how long they have been around.

sections.title: Estimating Conditions and Setting Parameters
sections.content:
At the end of each stabilization period, before restarting the timer, peers MUST recalculate three estimates: overlay size N, failure rate U and join rate L.

  • Size: since identifiers are spread uniformly, the average distance between identifiers in the neighborhood tells a peer how many peers exist. The RFC says this has been found accurate within 15%.
  • Failure rate: each peer keeps a history of the last K failures and divides the failure count by the routing table size times the time span of the history. K of 25% of the routing table size is RECOMMENDED. Failures are recorded when a Leave arrives or when a Ping goes unanswered after 2*Tr seconds of silence, where Tr defaults to 15 seconds. Using frequent extra messages instead is NOT RECOMMENDED.
  • Join rate: estimated from the ages of peers in the routing table, using the uptimes carried in Update and Probe messages. The RFC reports accuracy within 22%.

Routing table sizes follow from N. The finger table MUST be max(ceiling(log2(N)), 16). The successor list MUST be at most ceiling(log2(N)), and an implementation may set a lower limit such as three. The predecessor list MUST be ceiling(log2(N)).

The stabilization interval is the smaller of two values: one derived from the failure rate (time for N/2 peers to fail, divided by the square of log2(N)) and one from the join rate (time for N peers to join, divided by the same factor). Because too small an interval makes the overlay less stable, a lower limit of 15 s is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: Each kid guesses how big the group is, how fast kids are leaving and how fast new ones arrive. Then they pick a checking schedule that is not too lazy and not too nervous, and never faster than every 15 seconds.

sections.title: Sharing Estimates Between Peers
sections.content:
To make estimates more accurate, peers share them. When the stabilization timer fires, a peer sends a Probe request to number-of-peers-to-probe random peers from its finger table. Fingers are used rather than neighbors because neighbors are likely to make similar errors. Both the Probe and its answer MUST carry a message extension of type self_tuning_data with critical set to False.

The extension holds a SelfTuningData structure with the sender's latest network_size, join_rate and leave_rate. Rates are expressed per 24 hours, rounded up.

During each interval a peer stores the estimates it receives. At the end it uses the 75th percentile (third quartile) of its own estimate plus the received ones. The default of 4 probes gives a peer about nine estimates on average, and a value below 4 is NOT RECOMMENDED. The element self-tuning:number-of-peers-to-probe is added to each configuration element of the overlay configuration document, and its namespace goes in the mandatory-extension element.
sections.eli5: The kids compare notes with a few friends across the circle, then take a fairly high guess from all the answers so one odd answer cannot throw things off.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Malicious or compromised peers could already advertise false metrics or routing information under RELOAD base, and in the same way they could share false size, join rate and leave rate estimates. The same security concerns apply. As long as the number of malicious peers stays modest, using the 75th percentile keeps clearly different estimates from having much influence.

An attacker who can impersonate many peers in strategic locations could send enough false estimates to influence a victim's choice of stabilization interval.

IANA registers the self_tuning_data extension (code 0x3) in the RELOAD Extensions Registry, the overlay algorithm name CHORD-SELF-TUNING, and the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:p2p:self-tuning.
sections.eli5: A sneaky kid could tell lies about how busy the group is. Taking a high-but-not-highest guess from many answers makes a few liars less powerful, though not a crowd of fake kids.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH PEER ESTIMATES AND TUNES

items.title: Overlay size N
items.text: From the density of identifiers among neighbors.

items.title: Failure rate U
items.text: From a history of the last K observed failures.

items.title: Join rate L
items.text: From the ages (uptimes) of peers in the routing table.

items.title: Stabilization interval
items.text: The smaller of the failure-based and join-based values.
